prompt: To compare two running shoe brands, each of $20$ runners runs a timed mile in Brand X and a timed mile in Brand Y, with the order decided by a coin flip for each runner. Which design is this, and what is its advantage?

choices.label: Completely randomized design; it is the simplest to run
Matched pairs design; each runner is their own control, so runner-to-runner differences are removed from the comparison
Observational study; the runners chose their own shoes
Cluster sample; the runners were grouped by brand

hint: Every runner tries BOTH treatments. That is the fingerprint of one specific design.

hints.text: Every runner tries BOTH treatments. That is the fingerprint of one specific design.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Warm up: a fast runner in X and a slow runner in Y tells you nothing about the shoes. But the SAME runner in X then Y, compared, cancels out that runner's ability. That is the whole idea.
Comparing each runner's two times is a matched pairs design. The coin flip randomizes the order so practice or fatigue does not favor one brand.
Matched pairs, and the advantage is removing runner-to-runner variability: choice B.

explanation: Each runner receives both treatments, and the two times for that runner are compared. This is a matched pairs design, a special block design where each subject is a block.
Runners vary hugely in speed. By comparing a runner only with themselves, that variability is removed, making a real shoe difference much easier to detect.
Randomizing the order of X and Y controls for warm-up and fatigue. Choice B.

alternativeExplanations.title: How the analysis changes
steps: Instead of comparing the 20 X-times with the 20 Y-times as two groups, compute each runner's difference (X time minus Y time).
You get 20 differences, and the question becomes "is the average difference zero?"
This is the paired-data method that returns in the inference units.

alternativeExplanations.title: The trap in choice A
steps: A completely randomized design would give 10 runners Brand X and 10 Brand Y, once each.
Here nobody is assigned to one brand; everyone does both.
Only the ORDER is randomized, which is the signature of matched pairs.
